title: From Wallets to Super Apps: The Internet's New Interface (with Phantom CEO)
abstract:
PART 1 — ABSTRACT

This conversation centers on the evolution of crypto wallets as the foundational interface for a new, decentralized financial internet, positioning them as potential "super apps" that anchor user experiences around finance before expanding into broader services. The discussion highlights why wallets are uniquely suited to fill this role: they solve the hardest problem first—managing money, compliance, and trust—unlike social or messaging apps that tack financial features on as secondary. This matters as wallets could shape the next generation of institutional and consumer finance, driving adoption and changing how users interact with financial products. Unresolved questions include whether crypto wallets can overcome remaining UX challenges, how broadly they can serve mainstream needs beyond speculation and trading, and what role AI or curation will play in the next phase of users’ financial interactions.

PART 2 — KEY IDEAS

- Crypto wallets are emerging as the de facto entry point to the on-chain ecosystem, acting as both key managers and increasingly full-featured financial platforms.
- Starting from finance gives wallets a strategic advantage in becoming super apps—a contrast to Western consumer apps that struggled to add payments/functionality after achieving adoption through social or utility.
- The space is fragmenting: some wallets are developer platforms supporting third-party mini-apps, while others, like Phantom, are more opinionated, building directly integrated features catering to major user trends.
- Building user trust, simplifying complex financial tools (e.g., perpetuals), and enhancing onboarding are crucial to breaking down barriers for everyday users.
- The interoperability of wallets (users can import the same seed phrase into multiple apps) fosters competition on experience and security, but real-world stickiness comes from user trust and brand, not switching convenience.
- Product development in wallets prioritizes curation—focusing only on trends and features with sustainable, long-term value, despite the temptation to chase short-term gains.
- Mainstream adoption is still gated by the ability to abstract away complexity (e.g., social logins, transaction simulation, risk customization) and pivot towards functions like payments and social finance, not just speculation.
- Social features are being integrated to enhance discovery and engagement, drawing inspiration from fintech “activity feeds” (e.g., Venmo) rather than pure social networks.
- Institutional implications include the possibility for wallets to unlock global financial access in ways that traditional fintechs like Robinhood cannot, due to crypto’s permissionless, borderless nature.
- The potential intersection of AI and wallets raises questions about the evolving UX, with speculation that wallets (or agents) may eventually automate and curate user financial decisions—though trust and adoption remain hurdles.
